mainEntity.name: Is it painful to have a veneer replaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: The process of replacing a veneer is typically carried out under local anaesthesia, so discomfort during the procedure itself is generally minimal. Some patients experience mild sensitivity in the days following replacement, particularly if the underlying tooth has been exposed. Your dental team will advise on appropriate aftercare to help manage any temporary sensitivity. Every patient's experience differs, and your dentist will discuss what to expect based on your specific clinical situation before proceeding.

mainEntity.name: Can a chipped veneer be repaired rather than replaced?

acceptedAnswer.text: In some cases — particularly with composite veneers — minor chips can be repaired by adding and sculpting additional composite resin material to the affected area. However, matching the original shade exactly can be challenging over time as materials age differently. Porcelain veneers, when chipped, more commonly require full replacement rather than repair, as the material is more difficult to add to predictably. Your dentist will assess the extent of the damage and advise on the most appropriate option.

mainEntity.name: Will my teeth look different once my veneers are removed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the tooth surface is lightly prepared (a small amount of enamel is typically removed) during the original veneer placement, the tooth may look slightly different once a veneer is removed. This is one reason why teeth that have had veneers placed generally need to remain covered with a restoration of some kind. Your dentist will discuss this aspect of treatment with you during any consultation about replacement options.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if there is decay under my veneer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Decay beneath a veneer is not always visible to the naked eye in its early stages. It may present as a dark shadow at the margin, persistent sensitivity, or a change in sensation when biting. In many cases, dental X-rays are needed to assess the area beneath and around the veneer accurately. This is another reason why regular dental check-ups are important for patients with veneers — early detection of any changes allows for more conservative management.

mainEntity.name: Does the NHS cover veneer replacement?

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain veneers are generally considered a cosmetic dental treatment and are not routinely available on the NHS. Composite veneers may occasionally be provided on the NHS in specific clinical circumstances, but this varies. For most patients seeking veneer replacement or new veneers for cosmetic reasons, this will be arranged through private dental care. It is worth discussing costs and treatment options openly with your dental practice during your consultation.

mainEntity.name: How can I find a suitable dentist in the City of London for veneer assessment?

acceptedAnswer.text: If you are based in or near the City of London and have concerns about existing veneers, seeking a consultation with a dental practice experienced in cosmetic restorative dentistry is a sensible first step. A thorough clinical examination will allow the dentist to assess the current condition of your veneers, identify any concerns, and explain your options clearly. Look for a practice registered with the Care Quality Commission (CQC) and where treating dentists are registered with the General Dental Council (GDC).
